months.title: System Design Basics + Real RAG (Flagship Project #1)
months.focus: This is the month your AI story gets genuinely strong. You already know exactly what Physynex's retrieval system needs to do — you specified it — but it was AI-assisted, not hand-built. Now you build the same thing yourself, with real infrastructure this time.

tasks.text: Trees (~10 problems)
System design: scalability, caching, load balancing, CAP theorem (concepts only)
Embeddings deep-dive: how they're generated, what "similarity" means, chunking strategies
Trees cont. (~8 problems)
Practice designing: URL shortener, rate limiter (write it out, don't just read about it)
Vector databases: start with Chroma (fastest path to a working prototype)
Tries + Heap (~10 problems)
Practice designing: a basic chat app backend
LangChain fundamentals — retrieval chains, document loaders
Heap cont. + review (~5 problems)
Build: rebuild Physynex's retrieval pipeline yourself, from scratch, with a real vector database — same requirements, your own code this time

months.projectText: This is a genuine from-scratch build, not a refactor. You already know the spec cold (you directed it) — now you implement every piece yourself for the first time: chunking, embedding calls, similarity search, guardrail logic, red-flag detection. Don't build it inside Physynex's private codebase. Build it as a separate, standalone, public repo — a small reusable RAG engine (chunking + embedding + Chroma/pgvector retrieval) — then wire it into Physynex once it works. Two wins at once: the hands-on RAG skill you're actually missing, and a genuinely public, well-documented repo with real production usage behind it, which solves a gap you have on GitHub right now (more in Part 6).

milestones.text: ~35 more DSA problems (cumulative ~110–115)
Can whiteboard 3 classic system designs out loud, unscripted
A working, public RAG repo you wrote yourself, with a real vector database, integrated into a live product
Can defend every implementation choice — chunking strategy, embedding trade-offs, guardrail logic — because you wrote it this time, not just explain what it's supposed to do

### MONTH 4 — AI Agents + Advanced Full-Stack (Flagship Project #2)

**Focus:** Move from "retrieves information" to "takes action." This is the differentiator that shows up explicitly in senior AI job postings (tool use, agentic libraries, MCP) — you're building the junior version of that now.

**Project — Flagship #2:** Give your AI assistant the ability to *act*, not just answer. Two options — pick based on comfort experimenting on a live product:
- **Extend Physynex:** connect the assistant to your real booking system (check availability, book a slot) via tool calling — powerful because it's a real production feature with real constraints.
- **Standalone agent project:** if you'd rather not touch Physynex's production path yet, build a fresh agentic project in the same domain (a booking/scheduling agent, or a research/support agent) as its own public repo. Lower risk, same learning, still portfolio-worthy.

Either way: this is where MCP awareness pays off directly, since it's explicitly listed as a requirement in current senior full-stack-AI postings.

**Month 4 Milestone:**
- [ ] ~32 more DSA problems (cumulative ~142–147)

## Part 1 — Where You Stand Today

### 1.1 Strengths & Transferable Skills

These are real, and you should stop underselling them:

- **Production React/Next.js/TypeScript depth.** 65+ shipped components, Redux/Context refactors with a measured 30%+ maintainability gain, multiple *live* products (not tutorial projects). This is your floor, not your ceiling — it's already competitive.
- **Backend-adjacent range most "frontend" candidates don't have.** Node.js middleware design, the BFF pattern, secure API proxying (sanitization, token forwarding, header injection), Express. You already think about backend concerns — you just haven't formalized the database/testing/infra side yet.
- **Genuine product-level understanding of applied AI — still rare, even without the hands-on code yet.** You specified and directed exactly what a serious AI feature needs: retrieval logic (keyword + embeddings hybrid), topic/guardrail controls, red-flag symptom detection, lead classification. Most engineers never get this far — they either avoid AI features entirely or bolt on a raw API call with no product thinking. To be precise about where you actually stand (per your own correction): the Physynex implementation was AI-assisted, so the hands-on technical depth — writing the retrieval code yourself, defending every choice under questioning — isn't there yet. That's exactly what Months 3–4 rebuild, using Physynex's own requirements as the spec. Pulled from live job postings while researching this: an Accenture "AI/ML Engineer" listing (7.5 yrs min) and a remote "Senior Full Stack AI Engineer" role (₹22–30 LPA) both ask for this shape of work. You already understand the shape of the job — the roadmap builds the hands to match.
- **Full delivery-lifecycle exposure.** CI/CD (Jenkins), deployment, third-party integrations (HubSpot, Webflow, ZeroBounce).
- **Entrepreneurial/product range that's unusual at 2–3 years in.** Physynex and Croire Paints (croirepaints.com — a live 3D product showcase using Three.js/React Three Fiber, currently not on your resume) are real, live, customer-facing products you built and shipped, not internal-only assignments. This is strong behavioral-interview material.
- **You quantify everything.** 30%+, 25%, 20%, 15% — this is genuinely good resume practice and most candidates don't do it.

### 1.2 Gap Analysis — Full Stack Developer Track

Checked against your resume, your actual GitHub, and real "Full Stack Developer" postings on Indeed India (2–6 yrs band) as of July 2026:

| Gap | Why it matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL / relational databases** | Near-universal expectation alongside or instead of MongoDB. A live GLOINNT "Full Stack Developer (MERN/MEAN)" posting and a Carlton IT listing both explicitly wanted relational DB comfort, not just Mongo. | 0 mentions on resume |
| **Automated testing** | "Write clean, maintainable code and perform unit testing" appears directly in a real job description you're a strong fit for otherwise. | 0 mentions on resume/GitHub |
| **DSA / coding-interview fluency** | Still gates most Indian tech interviews regardless of role or seniority. | No LeetCode/competitive profile referenced |
| **System design fundamentals** | Standard from mid-level up; increasingly asked even at 2–3 YOE for product companies. | Not mentioned |
| **Docker** | Table-stakes for "owns a feature end-to-end" positioning. | Not mentioned |
| **One cloud platform (recommend AWS)** | Two of three detailed job postings pulled during research explicitly required AWS or Azure service familiarity, not just Jenkins CI/CD. | Not mentioned |

### 1.3 Gap Analysis — AI Engineering Track

| Gap | Why it matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Python** | The single biggest blocker. Every AI-adjacent posting pulled — Accenture's AI/ML Engineer role, the Gen AI Solutions Engineer role, the remote Full Stack AI Engineer role — lists Python as a must-have, often "advanced." Your resume has zero Python. | 0 mentions |
| **ML fundamentals (workflow-level)** | Not deep math — but you should be able to explain train/test splits, overfitting, evaluation metrics, and when classical ML beats an LLM call. | Not present |
| **Hands-on RAG implementation** | You directed and understand the concept (retrieval, guardrails, red-flagging, lead classification) — genuinely good product instinct — but the code itself was AI-assisted. Writing and defending the implementation yourself is the real gap, not just adding a vector database on top of something you already built by hand. Treat Month 3 as building the thing for the first time, not upgrading it. | Physynex's pipeline exists and works, but wasn't hand-built by you |
| **Agent frameworks + tool use** | Every mid-to-senior AI job posting checked (Accenture, CloudiQS) explicitly asks for agentic libraries — LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGen, or AWS's Strands/Bedrock AgentCore. | Not present |
| **Model Context Protocol (MCP) awareness** | As of mid-2026, MCP has become the standard tool-interoperability layer across essentially every major agent framework (LangGraph, CrewAI, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Strands) — and it's explicitly listed as a "must-have" in the CloudiQS senior posting. Worth knowing conceptually even before you're using it daily. | Not present |

### 1.4 Skill Tiers

**Essential (blocks you from being competitive without it):**
SQL/Postgres · Testing (Jest + RTL) · DSA · System design basics · Docker · One cloud platform · Python · Applied ML fundamentals · Real RAG with a vector database · Basic agent/tool-use pattern

**Recommended (strong differentiator, not a hard blocker):**
GitHub Actions CI/CD · Redis · WebSockets · Basic observability (error tracking/logging) · FastAPI (Python backend — several AI-engineer postings specifically want this alongside or instead of Node) · LangChain/LangGraph fluency · MCP hands-on · LLM evaluation basics · Fine-tuning concepts (conceptual, not hands-on)

**Optional (nice to have, don't chase these first):**
GraphQL · Kubernetes · React Native · Multi-cloud · Computer vision · Deep learning math / training models from scratch · Open-source contributions to third-party projects

### 1.5 Interview-Ready vs. Needs Significant Work

**Interview-ready right now:**
- React/JS/TS fundamentals, hooks, component architecture, state management patterns
- Node.js/Express, REST API design, middleware/auth/session concepts
- Explaining Physynex's AI assistant at the *product/architecture* level — what it does, why each piece exists (guardrails, red-flagging, lead classification) — you already have a 30-question prep document from an earlier session covering this and general React/JS/Node fundamentals; reuse and extend it, don't rebuild it
- Agile process questions, ownership/initiative stories (Physynex, Croire Paints)

**Needs significant work:**
- DSA in *timed coding-interview format* specifically (you code well on the job — that's a different skill from solving an unseen problem in 30 minutes)
- System design in whiteboard/verbal-reasoning format
- SQL (currently ~zero)
- Testing (currently ~zero)
- **Defending Physynex's RAG implementation at the code level** — right now, "walk me through how you built the retrieval logic" is a genuine risk area, because you can explain the *what* and *why* but not yet every implementation choice. This closes specifically in Month 3, once you've rebuilt it yourself.
- Python/ML/AI technical depth beyond the prompt-engineering level — you can't yet defend vector DB trade-offs, chunking strategy choices, or agent architecture decisions in an interview
- Cloud/deployment architecture depth (Jenkins CI/CD is real experience, but it's not the same as being able to reason about AWS service choices)

### 1.6 The Strategic Call: AI Engineer, Not ML Engineer

This distinction matters enough to state plainly, because it determines what you spend your limited hours on.

**ML Engineer / LLM Engineer** — trains, fine-tunes, and optimizes models from the inside. Requires real depth in linear algebra, probability/statistics, and frameworks like PyTorch/TensorFlow. Realistic timeline to competitive: 12–24+ months of focused study, often alongside formal coursework. Not what you're asking for, and not necessary for the roles your profile fits.

**AI Engineer** — takes existing foundation models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) via API and builds reliable, production-grade *systems* around them: RAG pipelines, agents, tool-calling workflows, evaluation harnesses. Requires strong software engineering (you have this), Python, and applied understanding of LLM behavior — not model internals. This is a software engineering job with an AI-shaped surface area, and it's the fastest, highest-upside move for someone already building production software, which is exactly your position.

Market data backs this, and not just from one source: current industry comparisons describe the field shifting hard toward AI engineer roles for working software engineers specifically *because* you keep everything you already know and layer applied-AI skills on top, rather than starting a new specialization from zero. Broader India-specific data points the same direction — a July 2026 hiring report tracking 18,400+ Indian tech listings found AI Engineer roles growing faster month-over-month than any other tracked role (+21%), averaging ₹18.8 LPA, with Bengaluru alone accounting for over a third of listings; separately, "AI-Integrated Full-Stack Developer" is now named explicitly as one of the highest-demand full-stack role categories in India for 2026, which is precisely the hybrid position this roadmap is built to get you into. That's this roadmap's entire bet. Every AI-track item below (Python, RAG, vector DBs, agents, MCP) is chosen because it serves the AI Engineer path — not the ML research path.

sections.contentMarkdown:
## Part 2 — Reality Check

### 2.1 What 6 Months Can Realistically Buy You

Being direct, as you asked:

- **Full Stack readiness: very achievable, close to done.** You're not starting from zero — you're closing five well-defined gaps (SQL, testing, DSA, system design, Docker/cloud) on top of a genuinely strong existing base. Six months at a sustainable pace comfortably gets you interview-ready across the mid-level Full Stack market.
- **"AI Engineer" (applied/product AI, RAG + agents): achievable and realistic.** This is a software-engineering skill layered on top of skills you already have. Six months is enough to build 2–3 genuinely strong, defensible AI-integrated projects and speak fluently about the concepts.
- **"ML Engineer" (training/fine-tuning models from scratch, research-depth math): not realistic in 6 months alongside a full-time job**, and — per the strategic call above — not the path that matches either your background or where the market is pulling. If a role explicitly demands this, it's outside this roadmap's scope; that's a 12–24 month investment with a different daily structure (much more math, much less shipping).
- **DSA depth vs. breadth.** ~180–200 problems over 6 months (detailed in Part 4) is a strong bar for mid-tier-and-above product companies and matches what most working engineers achieve in this timeframe. If you specifically target FAANG-tier companies, expect their bar to sit higher (often 300–400+ problems, refined over a longer window) — worth knowing now rather than discovering it in month 5.
- **Doing both tracks at once means slower depth in each** than focusing on one alone. The sequencing below is deliberately designed so Full Stack fundamentals (which you're closer to finishing) land first, and AI depth builds on top — so if time gets tight anywhere, you fall back to "strong Full Stack engineer with real applied-AI experience," which is itself a highly competitive, hard-to-fake position, not a failure state.

### 2.2 Your Weekly Time Budget

Built around 10 AM–7 PM weekdays (sometimes 8 PM), with burnout avoidance as a hard constraint — and restructured around single-subject focus per session, not split hours. That's the right call for technical material: switching subjects mid-session costs you the ramp-up time twice, and real understanding needs enough unbroken time to read/watch *and* immediately practice, not just skim two things shallowly.

| Day | Window | Focus (one subject, full session) | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 8:30–10:30 PM | DSA — full session | 2h |
| Tue | 8:30–10:30 PM | Full-Stack topic — full session | 2h |
| Wed | 8:30–10:30 PM | DSA — full session | 2h |
| Thu | 8:30–10:30 PM | AI/Python topic — full session | 2h |
| Fri | Flexible | Light DSA review, or fully off | 0–1h |
| Sat | Morning + afternoon | Project work — one continuous focus (the mid-session break is for rest, not for switching subjects) | 4h |
| Sun | Morning | One single-focus block, rotating weekly: DSA weak-spot review, OR extended theory/course video, OR extra project time — whichever the week needs most | 2.5h |
| Sun | End of session | Logistics only — plan next week. Not a learning task, so it doesn't break the single-focus rule | 0.5h |
| Sun | Afternoon/evening | Rest — protected, not optional | 0h |

**Total: ~15–16 hrs/week → ~65–70 hrs/month → ~400–420 hrs over 6 months.** Same total as the original design — this repackages the hours into deeper, uninterrupted blocks, it doesn't add hours.

**How this maps onto the month-by-month tables in Part 3:** the "DSA" column = your Monday + Wednesday sessions. The "Full-Stack" column = your Tuesday session. The "AI/Python" column = your Thursday session. Project work = mostly Saturday, with Sunday as overflow if something needs more room that week.

**On 8 PM days:** don't try to force the full 2h block in — shift to 9:00–10:30 PM (1.5h) and keep it single-subject, just shorter. A shorter uninterrupted block beats a full-length one chopped into two subjects.

**Non-negotiable:** at least one full day off per week (built in above as Sunday evening + flexible Friday). If you miss a day, don't double up the next day to "catch up" — just resume the plan. Catch-up cramming is the single most common cause of burnout-driven quitting in self-study plans like this one.

### 2.3 Trade-offs, Stated Plainly

1. **Depth vs. breadth in DSA:** you're optimizing for "strong at most companies," not "strongest possible at any company." If a specific FAANG-tier interview appears on your calendar, you'll want a 3–4 week intensive bump beyond this plan.
2. **AI Engineer vs. ML Engineer:** covered in 1.6 — this roadmap deliberately does not chase deep ML math or from-scratch model training. That's the right call for your timeline and background, but it does mean roles that specifically want research-level ML depth stay out of reach after 6 months.
3. **Two tracks, one calendar:** if a month runs short, Part 9 tells you exactly what to cut and what to protect. Full Stack fundamentals are protected first; the more exploratory AI-agent work is the first to compress.
4. **Simultaneous job interviewing:** Months 5–6 assume you're also actively interviewing, which eats into study time. That's intentional — the point of the roadmap is to get hired, not to keep studying indefinitely.

Checked directly (github.com/prasanthkrjha): 5 public repos — `BlogPage`, `Student-Enrollment-System`, `Weather-Update`, `dashboard-react`, `LandingPage`. These read as early-coursework projects. ## Part 7 — Interview Preparation

### 7.1 Technical Topics to Cover

**Full-stack conceptual (you're closer here than you think — extend, don't restart):**
React internals (reconciliation, rendering behavior, hooks rules, closures) · Node.js event loop · REST API design principles · database indexing & normalization · caching strategies (client, CDN, server, DB-level) · auth patterns (JWT vs. sessions) · CORS. You already have a 30-question interview-prep document from an earlier session covering React/JS fundamentals, the Node.js middleware/BFF pattern, and Gen AI/Physynex architecture at the conceptual level — treat that as your base layer for process and concept questions. Its Physynex answers cover the *what and why*; pair them with Month 3's rebuild so you can also answer the *how*, line by line, when someone digs in.

**AI/LLM conceptual (new ground — this is where you need the most reps):**
How RAG actually works end-to-end · chunking strategy trade-offs · when vector search beats keyword search (and when it doesn't) · embedding model selection trade-offs · hallucination mitigation approaches · prompt injection awareness (genuinely relevant to you — you already specified red-flag/guardrail detection for Physynex, so frame this as an extension of the security thinking you already demonstrated at the product level, now backed by Month 3's hands-on rebuild) · agent architecture patterns (the ReAct loop, tool calling, single-agent vs. multi-agent) · fine-tuning vs. RAG vs. prompting trade-offs.

**DSA & System Design:** covered in Parts 3 and 4.

### 7.2 Behavioral Preparation

Use the STAR method, and build your story bank from bullets you already have real evidence for:
- The Redux/Context refactor (30%+ maintainability) → *technical decision-making, code quality ownership*
- HubSpot/Webflow/ZeroBounce integration (25% efficiency) → *cross-functional collaboration, ambiguity*
- The Physynex retrieval pipeline (the original spec and direction) → *initiative, product thinking, translating a real user need (patient safety, lead quality) into AI feature requirements*
- The Month 3 rebuild and Month 4 agent-building work from this roadmap → *self-directed technical learning, closing your own gaps deliberately, growth mindset*
- Physynex and Croire Paints as products, not just codebases → *ownership, end-to-end thinking, entrepreneurial range*

### 7.3 Mock Interviews & Coding Practice Cadence

- **Months 1–4:** untimed DSA practice, focus on pattern recognition.
- **Month 5:** first mock interviews — Pramp (free, peer-matched) or Interviewing.io (free tier) for technical rounds; record yourself for behavioral answers and review the playback.
- **Month 6:** 1 mock interview per week minimum (technical, system design, or behavioral, rotating), plus timed LeetCode practice under interview conditions.
- Claude itself is a free, always-available option for drilling behavioral answers or talking through a system design out loud — useful between scheduled mocks, not a replacement for them.

sections.title: How to Use This Document
sections.contentMarkdown:
## How to Use This Document

- Each **Module** is a subject area. Each **Unit** inside it is one sitting's worth of learning — small enough to search for and finish, specific enough that the search actually returns the right thing.
- Every unit lists: the **exact concepts** inside it, the **primary resource** (verified, not guessed), a **secondary resource** if the first doesn't click, and what **"done" looks like** (problems solved / thing built / question you can now answer).
- **Tier** marks priority: 🔴 Essential (never skip) · 🟡 Recommended (strong differentiator) · 🟢 Optional (nice to have). Matches Part 9 of the roadmap — if time gets tight, drop 🟢 first, then 🟡, never 🔴.
- Sequencing matters — modules are numbered in the order that makes each one easiest to learn (e.g., SQL before RAG, Python before ML, RAG before Agents). Follow the order within a module; you can interleave modules the way the roadmap's calendar does.
- If a unit's resource isn't working for you, don't force it — the "if this doesn't land" search term is there specifically so you can find a second teacher without losing the thread.

# Complexity Analysis

Before you can compare two solutions to a problem, you need a shared language for "how fast" and "how much memory." That language is Big-O notation. Every DSA topic after this one assumes you can look at a loop and immediately say its complexity — so this unit is short, but skipping it makes everything downstream harder.

## What Big-O actually measures

Big-O describes how the **runtime or memory** of an algorithm grows as the input size (`n`) grows — not the exact number of operations, just the growth trend. We drop constants and lower-order terms because they stop mattering at scale: `O(2n)` and `O(n + 100)` are both just `O(n)`.

Common complexities, from fastest to slowest growth:

| Notation | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Constant | array index access, hashmap lookup |
| O(log n) | Logarithmic | binary search |
| O(n) | Linear | single loop over an array |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | efficient sorting (merge sort, quicksort avg case) |
| O(n²) | Quadratic | nested loops over the same input |
| O(2ⁿ) | Exponential | naive recursive Fibonacci, brute-force subsets |
| O(n!) | Factorial | brute-force permutations |

## Time vs. space complexity

**Time complexity** counts operations relative to `n`. **Space complexity** counts extra memory your algorithm allocates relative to `n` — this includes recursion call-stack depth, not just arrays you explicitly create. A recursive function with no extra arrays can still be `O(n)` space if it recurses `n` levels deep.

## Best, average, and worst case

The same algorithm can have different complexities depending on the input shape:

```js
function findTarget(arr, target) {
  for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] === target) return i; // best case: O(1), target is first
  }
  return -1; // worst case: O(n), target is absent or last
}
```

Interviewers almost always want **worst-case** complexity unless they say otherwise — average case matters more for things like hash tables (average O(1) lookup, worst case O(n) with pathological collisions).

## How to analyze a piece of code quickly

1. Find the loops. A single loop over `n` items is O(n). Two nested independent loops over `n` is O(n²).
2. Loops that halve the search space each time (binary search, balanced tree descent) are O(log n).
3. Recursion: multiply the number of recursive calls per level by the number of levels. Fibonacci's naive recursion branches twice per call, `n` levels deep → O(2ⁿ).
4. Hashmap/hashset operations (get, set, has) are O(1) average — this is the single most common way a brute-force O(n²) solution becomes O(n).

## Practice tip

Whenever you finish a problem, say its time and space complexity out loud before moving on. This habit is what makes complexity analysis automatic by the time you're in a real interview.

# SQL Fundamentals

SQL is the one skill your gap analysis flagged as "near-universal" — almost every Full Stack posting expects it regardless of whether the product uses Postgres, MySQL, or something else. This unit covers the core query vocabulary.

## SELECT and the anatomy of a query

```sql
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
GROUP BY column1
HAVING aggregate_condition
ORDER BY column1
LIMIT 10;
```

Logical execution order (not written order!): `FROM` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`. This is why you can't reference a `SELECT` alias in `WHERE`, but you can in `ORDER BY` — `WHERE` runs before the alias exists, `ORDER BY` runs after.

## JOIN types

```sql
-- INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all rows from the left table, matched data from the right (NULL if no match)
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;

-- RIGHT JOIN: mirror of LEFT — all rows from the right table
-- FULL JOIN: all rows from both sides, matched where possible
```

Mental model: **INNER** = intersection, **LEFT/RIGHT** = "keep everything from this side, fill gaps with NULL," **FULL** = union of both. `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` is the standard idiom for "find users with no orders."

## WHERE vs. GROUP BY vs. HAVING

`WHERE` filters **individual rows** before grouping. `HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregation — you need `HAVING` (not `WHERE`) to filter on an aggregate like `COUNT(*)` or `SUM(total)`:

```sql
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'   -- filters rows first
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;         -- filters groups after counting
```

## Aggregate functions

`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` collapse many rows into one value per group. Without `GROUP BY`, they collapse the **entire table** into a single row.

## Subqueries

A query nested inside another, usable in `WHERE`, `FROM`, or `SELECT`:

```sql
-- Find users who have placed at least one order
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders);
```

Subqueries are often rewritable as JOINs (and vice versa) — JOINs are usually faster since the query planner can optimize them better, but subqueries are often more readable for "does X exist" checks.

## Practice tip

Don't just read SQL — write queries against a real schema (your Postgres setup from Month 1). Reading `LEFT JOIN` syntax and *predicting* what a query returns before running it is what actually builds the skill.

# PostgreSQL & Database Design

Knowing SQL syntax is half the job; designing a schema that doesn't fall apart under real usage is the other half. This unit is about the design decisions that separate a "tutorial schema" from one you'd defend in a system design interview.

## Primary and foreign keys

A **primary key** uniquely identifies a row (`id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY`, or a UUID). A **foreign key** references another table's primary key, enforcing that the referenced row must actually exist:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  total NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
```

This is what prevents an `orders` row from ever pointing at a `user_id` that doesn't exist — the database rejects the insert instead of your application silently creating orphaned data.

## Normalization (1NF → 3NF)

Normalization is about eliminating redundancy so updates don't require touching the same fact in multiple places:

- **1NF:** every column holds a single atomic value (no comma-separated lists in a cell).
- **2NF:** every non-key column depends on the **whole** primary key, not just part of it (relevant for composite keys).
- **3NF:** every non-key column depends **only** on the primary key, not on another non-key column. Example violation: storing both `user_id` and `user_email` on an `orders` table — email depends on the user, not on the order, so it belongs only in `users`.

In practice: normalize by default, then deliberately **denormalize** specific columns later if you have a measured read-performance problem — don't start denormalized "for speed" before you have evidence you need it.

## Indexing

An index is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets Postgres find rows matching a condition without scanning the whole table:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
```

Add indexes on columns you frequently filter (`WHERE`), join (`ON`), or sort (`ORDER BY`) by. The trade-off: indexes speed up reads but slow down writes slightly (every insert/update must also update the index) and take extra disk space — so don't index every column reflexively.

## Transactions

A transaction groups multiple statements so they either **all** succeed or **all** roll back — critical for anything involving multiple related writes (e.g. deducting inventory and creating an order):

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = 42;
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id) VALUES (7, 42);
COMMIT; -- or ROLLBACK if something failed
```

Without a transaction, a crash between the two statements leaves your data inconsistent (inventory decremented but no order recorded).

## Practice tip

Design a schema for something you'd actually use — not a Mario database from a tutorial. Add foreign keys and at least one index, then intentionally try to insert bad data and watch Postgres reject it. That failure is the feature.

# Redis & Caching

Caching is one of the highest-leverage performance techniques in a system — and one of the easiest to misuse. This unit covers the mental model, not just the API.

## Key-value caching

Redis stores everything as key → value, entirely in memory, which makes reads and writes extremely fast (sub-millisecond) compared to a disk-backed database:

```
SET user:42:profile '{"name":"Prasanth","plan":"pro"}'
GET user:42:profile
DEL user:42:profile
```

The trade-off for that speed: memory is finite and (by default) not durable the way a database is — Redis is a cache and ephemeral store first, not your system of record.

## TTL / expiry

Every cached key can have a time-to-live after which Redis automatically evicts it — essential for anything that goes stale (session tokens, rate-limit counters, "trending" lists):

```
SET session:abc123 "user-42" EX 3600   -- expires in 1 hour
TTL session:abc123                       -- check remaining seconds
```

Without a TTL, a cache silently accumulates stale data forever — this is a common production bug: someone caches something "temporarily" and forgets the expiry.

## Cache-aside pattern

The most common caching strategy: your application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads from the real database, then **writes that result back into the cache** for next time.

```js
async function getUser(id) {
  const cached = await redis.get(`user:${id}`);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const user = await db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  await redis.set(`user:${id}`, JSON.stringify(user), "EX", 300);
  return user;
}
```

The database remains the source of truth; the cache is a disposable speed layer that can be wiped and rebuilt at any time without losing real data.

## When caching helps vs. hides a real problem

Caching genuinely helps when: the same data is read far more often than it changes, and recomputing/refetching it is expensive relative to how cheap a cache hit is. Caching becomes a trap when it's used to paper over a slow query or a bad schema instead of fixing the root cause — you end up with two sources of truth that can silently drift apart (**cache invalidation** is famously one of the two hard problems in computer science). A good rule: profile first, cache the specific hot path you measured, and always have a clear invalidation strategy (TTL, explicit delete-on-write, or both) before you ship it.

## Practice tip

Add a Redis cache in front of one real, slightly-slow query in a project you've built. Measure the response time before and after — that measured number is worth more in an interview than reciting the cache-aside pattern from memory.

# Docker

Docker is table-stakes for "owns a feature end-to-end" positioning — it's the difference between "runs on my machine" and a reproducible, deployable unit.

## Images vs. containers

An **image** is a read-only template (your app's code + runtime + dependencies, frozen at a point in time). A **container** is a running instance of an image — you can start many containers from the same image, each isolated from the others. The analogy: image is a class, container is an instance of that class.

## Dockerfile syntax

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

Order matters for build speed: `COPY package*.json` and `RUN npm ci` happen **before** `COPY . .` so Docker can cache the (usually slower) dependency-install layer and only re-run it when `package.json` actually changes — not on every source-code edit.

## Docker Compose (multi-container apps)

Compose defines and runs multiple related containers (your app + a database + Redis) together, with one command:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data:
```

Notice the app connects to `db` — Compose gives each service a DNS name matching its key, so containers can reach each other by name instead of hardcoded IPs.

## Volumes

Container filesystems are ephemeral by default — delete the container, lose the data. A **volume** persists data outside the container's lifecycle (`db-data` above), which is why the database's actual data survives `docker compose down` and comes back on `docker compose up`.

## Basic networking

By default, Compose puts all services in one project on a shared network, so `app` can reach `db:5432` without any extra configuration. Exposing a port to your host machine (`"3000:3000"`) is a separate concern from inter-container networking — you only need host port mapping for whatever you actually access from outside Docker (usually just the app, not the database).

## Practice tip

Containerize an existing Node/Next app end-to-end: write the Dockerfile, add Postgres via Compose, and get the app talking to the database entirely inside Docker. That full loop — not just `docker run hello-world` — is what Month 2's project actually asks for.

# AWS Fundamentals

You don't need to know all of AWS — you need to know the handful of services that come up in almost every "one cloud platform" requirement, and how they fit together.

## EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)

A virtual machine you rent by the hour (or second) — the closest AWS equivalent to "a Linux server you SSH into." You choose an instance type (CPU/RAM tradeoff), an AMI (the OS image it boots from), and a security group (firewall rules for inbound/outbound traffic). EC2 is the most flexible option and also the one requiring the most manual ops work (patching, scaling, process management) compared to managed alternatives.

## S3 (Simple Storage Service)

Object storage — think "a folder in the cloud with effectively unlimited capacity," not a filesystem you mount. You store and retrieve whole objects (files) by key, typically over HTTPS. Common uses: static assets, file uploads, backups, and as the origin for a CDN. S3 is not a database — don't reach for it when you need to query/filter structured data.

## IAM (Identity and Access Management) basics

IAM controls **who can do what** across your AWS account. Core concepts:

- **Users** — an identity for a person or service.
- **Roles** — a set of permissions that can be **assumed** temporarily (e.g. an EC2 instance assumes a role to read from S3, without embedding permanent credentials in code).
- **Policies** — JSON documents that grant or deny specific actions on specific resources.

The principle to internalize: **least privilege** — grant only the specific permissions a service actually needs, not broad admin access, because a compromised credential with narrow permissions does far less damage.

## VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) basics

A VPC is your own isolated network within AWS — you define IP ranges, subnets (public vs. private), and routing rules. A **public subnet** has a route to the internet (for things like a load balancer); a **private subnet** doesn't (for things like a database, which should never be directly internet-reachable). You won't design complex VPCs at this stage, but you should be able to explain why a database sits in a private subnet and a web server sits in a public one.

## Elastic Beanstalk

A "platform as a service" layer on top of EC2/S3/load-balancing/auto-scaling — you upload your code, and Beanstalk handles provisioning the underlying infrastructure. It trades some flexibility for a much gentler on-ramp than manually wiring EC2 + load balancer + auto-scaling group yourself. A reasonable first deployment target before you're ready to manage raw EC2 infrastructure directly.

## Free-tier limits

AWS's free tier has real caps (e.g. 750 hours/month of a `t2.micro` or `t3.micro` EC2 instance, 5GB of S3 standard storage) — know roughly what they are so you don't get a surprise bill, and so you can reason in an interview about what a workload would cost in production versus what's free to experiment with.

## Practice tip

Before touching AWS hands-on (Unit 4.3), be able to explain in one sentence each: what EC2 is, what S3 is, why IAM roles beat hardcoded credentials, and why a database belongs in a private subnet. That vocabulary is what lets the hands-on deployment click instead of feeling like following a script.

# AWS Hands-On Deployment

This unit is where 4.1 (Docker) and 4.2 (AWS fundamentals) stop being separate concepts and become one working, live-on-the-internet system. There's no substitute for actually doing this once, start to finish.

## The end-to-end shape

1. **Containerize** your app (Dockerfile from 4.1), and confirm it runs correctly locally via `docker build` + `docker run`.
2. **Provision** compute — either a raw EC2 instance (install Docker on it yourself, `docker run` your image) or Elastic Beanstalk (upload the Dockerized app, let Beanstalk handle the underlying EC2 + load balancer + scaling).
3. **Configure networking** — open the right inbound port in the security group (typically 80/443, proxied to your app's internal port), and point a domain or use the provided AWS URL.
4. **Handle environment/config** — database URL, API keys, and other secrets should come from environment variables set on the instance/Beanstalk environment, never baked into the Docker image itself.
5. **Verify** — hit the live URL from a browser on a different network than the one you deployed from, to confirm it's genuinely public, not just reachable from your own machine.

## A gentler on-ramp: Render or Railway first

If AWS's surface area feels like too much to debug all at once, deploying to Render or Railway first (both take a Dockerfile or a Git repo directly, with far less configuration) validates that your **app and Dockerfile** are correct before you also have to debug AWS-specific networking/IAM issues. Once that's confirmed working, redoing the same deployment on AWS isolates what's actually AWS-specific.

## Common failure points (and what they usually mean)

- **Can't reach the app at all:** almost always a security-group inbound rule blocking the port, not an application bug.
- **App starts but crashes immediately in the cloud, works locally:** almost always a missing environment variable (database URL, API key) that was only ever set in your local `.env` file.
- **Database connection refused:** check whether the database is reachable from the app's subnet/security group — a private-subnet database is often unreachable to instances outside its own VPC configuration by design.
- **Works, then stops after a redeploy:** check whether you're relying on the container's local filesystem for anything that needs to persist (uploaded files, SQLite databases) — container filesystems are ephemeral unless backed by a volume or moved to S3/RDS.

## Why this project matters more than it looks

"I deployed something to AWS once" and "I can explain exactly what happens between a browser request and my app responding, across DNS, load balancer, security group, and container" are very different levels of readiness — and the second one is what actually gets tested when a system design interview asks you to reason about a request's path through a real architecture.

## Practice tip

Don't stop at "it works." Intentionally break one thing — close the security group's port, or unset an environment variable — and diagnose the resulting failure from the symptoms alone. That debugging loop is where the real learning happens, not the initial successful deploy.
lessons.4.4:
# CI/CD & Observability

Shipping code manually doesn't scale, and you can't fix what you can't see failing. This unit covers the automation and visibility layer that sits on top of a working deployment.

## GitHub Actions pipeline stages

A CI/CD pipeline typically has three stages, each gating the next:

```yaml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build-test-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Test
        run: npm test

      - name: Deploy
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: ./deploy.sh
```

- **Build:** does the code even compile/bundle successfully?
- **Test:** does it behave correctly (unit + integration tests from Module 3)?
- **Deploy:** only runs if build and test both passed, and typically only on the main branch — this is what prevents broken code from ever reaching production, because a failing step stops the pipeline before deploy runs.

## Why this matters beyond convenience

CI/CD isn't just "automating a chore" — it's a correctness gate. Every push gets the same build+test treatment regardless of who wrote it or how confident they felt, which is exactly the kind of consistency a solo developer's memory can't reliably provide.

## Structured logging

Plain `console.log("something happened")` is nearly useless once you have real traffic — you can't search, filter, or correlate it. Structured logging emits logs as consistent key-value data (usually JSON):

```js
logger.info("order_created", { userId: 42, orderId: 1001, total: 59.99 });
```

This makes logs queryable: "show me every `order_created` event for `userId: 42` in the last hour" is a real query against structured logs, but not against free-text strings.

## Error tracking (Sentry-style)

An error-tracking service automatically captures unhandled exceptions in production — with the stack trace, the request context, and the ability to group repeated occurrences of the same underlying bug into one issue instead of one alert per occurrence:

```js
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";
Sentry.init({ dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN });

app.use(Sentry.Handlers.errorHandler());
```

Without this, the first person to learn about a production bug is often a user complaining — with it, you learn about it the moment it happens, with enough context to actually fix it.

## Recognizing why this is a "recommended," not "essential," tier item

Structured logging and error tracking meaningfully differentiate a candidate ("this person thinks about production, not just shipping"), but you can be interview-competent without hands-on Sentry experience — whereas skipping DSA or SQL entirely is a hard blocker. Prioritize accordingly if time gets tight (see Part 9's priority order).

## Practice tip

Add basic structured logging and one error-tracking integration to a project you've already deployed (Month 2's Docker+cloud project is the natural target) — seeing a real error show up in a dashboard, with a stack trace and request context, is what makes this concept concrete instead of abstract.
lessons.5.1:
# Core Concepts (System Design)

Every system design answer, no matter the specific question, draws on the same handful of core trade-offs. Get these solid before touching specific "design X" problems.

## Vertical vs. horizontal scaling

**Vertical scaling** (scale up): give one machine more CPU/RAM. Simple, but has a hard ceiling (there's a biggest machine you can buy) and creates a single point of failure. **Horizontal scaling** (scale out): add more machines and distribute load across them. More complex (now you need load balancing, and your app must be stateless or share state externally), but scales much further and improves fault tolerance — losing one of ten machines is a blip, not an outage.

The general industry direction for anything expected to grow: design for horizontal scaling from the start, even if you only run one instance today.

## CAP theorem

In a distributed system, when a network partition occurs (some nodes can't talk to others), you must choose between:

- **Consistency** — every read gets the most recent write, or an error.
- **Availability** — every request gets a response, even if it might not reflect the latest write.

You can't have both **during a partition** (you can always have both when the network is healthy — CAP is specifically about the partition case). This is why different databases make different defaults: traditional relational databases lean CP (reject requests rather than serve stale data), many NoSQL stores lean AP (serve slightly stale data rather than error out). Knowing which one your system needs — "would you rather show a slightly outdated cart, or show an error?" — is the actual interview-relevant skill, not reciting the acronym.

## Latency vs. throughput

**Latency** is how long a single request takes. **Throughput** is how many requests the system handles per unit time. These aren't the same axis — a system can have low latency but low throughput (fast per-request, but can't handle many at once), or high throughput but higher latency (batches requests to process many at once, at the cost of per-request speed, like a queue-based system). Optimizing for one can hurt the other; know which one a given problem actually cares about before proposing a solution.

## Availability

Usually expressed as a percentage of uptime ("three nines" = 99.9%, "five nines" = 99.999%). Each additional nine is dramatically harder and more expensive to achieve — 99.9% allows about 8.7 hours of downtime a year, 99.999% allows about 5 minutes. Redundancy (no single point of failure) is the core technique: multiple instances behind a load balancer, database replicas, multi-region deployment for the most demanding cases.

## How to use these in an interview

These four ideas are your **vocabulary**, not your answer. A strong system design response names the relevant trade-off explicitly ("this is a CP choice — we're prioritizing consistency because double-charging a customer is worse than a brief unavailability") rather than just listing components. Practice narrating the trade-off out loud, not just drawing the diagram.
lessons.5.2:
# Networking & APIs (System Design)

Once you've internalized the core trade-offs (5.1), this unit is about the specific components that sit between a client and your application logic.

## Load balancers

A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple backend instances — the component that actually makes horizontal scaling work in practice. Common strategies: round-robin (rotate evenly), least-connections (send to whichever instance has the fewest active requests), and IP-hash (same client consistently routed to the same instance, useful when you need session affinity). A load balancer also does health checks, automatically routing around instances that stop responding — this is a big part of how a system stays available when one server dies.

## API gateways

A single entry point that sits in front of multiple backend services, handling cross-cutting concerns once instead of in every service: authentication, rate limiting, request routing, and sometimes response aggregation (combining calls to multiple internal services into one client-facing response). This becomes especially relevant once you have more than one backend service — without a gateway, every service has to reimplement auth and rate limiting independently.

## REST vs. RPC vs. GraphQL

- **REST** — resources identified by URLs, manipulated via HTTP verbs (`GET /users/42`, `POST /orders`). Simple, cacheable (HTTP caching works naturally), but can lead to over-fetching (getting fields you don't need) or under-fetching (needing multiple round trips for related data).
- **RPC** (e.g. gRPC) — call a function on a remote service as if it were local (`getUser(42)`). Often faster (binary protocol, strongly typed contracts) and a natural fit for internal service-to-service communication, less natural for public-facing APIs consumed by arbitrary clients.
- **GraphQL** — the client specifies exactly which fields it needs in a single query, solving over/under-fetching, at the cost of more complex server-side implementation and harder HTTP-level caching (most requests are POSTs to one endpoint).

Know the trade-off, not just the definitions: REST is the safe, simple default; GraphQL earns its complexity when clients have very different, unpredictable data needs (e.g. a public API used by many different frontends); RPC wins for internal, performance-sensitive service-to-service calls.

## Rate limiting

Protects a system from being overwhelmed — by a bug, a traffic spike, or abuse — by capping how many requests a client can make in a given window. Common algorithms:

- **Token bucket** — a bucket refills with tokens at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token; requests are rejected when the bucket is empty. Allows short bursts up to the bucket size.
- **Sliding window** — counts requests in a rolling time window, giving smoother enforcement than a fixed window (which can allow 2x the intended rate right at a window boundary).

"Design a rate limiter" is one of the classic system design interview questions precisely because it's small enough to fully design in 30–45 minutes while still touching real trade-offs (memory vs. accuracy, distributed vs. single-instance state).

## Practice tip

For each concept here, be ready to answer "why would I choose this over the alternative?" — that comparative framing is what interviewers are actually listening for, more than definitions recited in isolation.
lessons.5.3:
# Data & Storage at Scale

Once a system outgrows a single database on a single machine, a new set of trade-offs shows up — this unit is about the vocabulary for that transition.

## SQL vs. NoSQL trade-offs

**SQL** (relational) databases give you strong consistency, joins, and enforced schema/relationships — ideal when your data is genuinely relational and correctness (no orphaned or contradictory records) matters more than raw write throughput. **NoSQL** databases (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) trade some of that structure for horizontal scalability and flexible schemas — ideal when you need to scale writes massively, your data doesn't fit a rigid relational shape, or you're optimizing for a specific access pattern (e.g. a key-value store for session data). Neither is universally "better" — the right interview answer names the actual access pattern and consistency needs of the specific system being designed, not a blanket preference.

## Replication

Copying data across multiple database instances, for two reasons: **fault tolerance** (if the primary dies, a replica can take over) and **read scaling** (route read traffic across multiple replicas instead of hammering one instance). The common pattern is single-primary replication: all writes go to one primary, which asynchronously (or synchronously) propagates changes to replicas. Asynchronous replication is faster but has a "replication lag" window where a replica might briefly serve stale data — relevant to the CAP theorem trade-off from 5.1.

## Sharding / partitioning

Splitting one logical dataset **across multiple database instances**, each holding a subset of the data (as opposed to replication, where each instance holds a full copy). A common approach: shard by a key (e.g. `user_id % number_of_shards`, or a hash of the key) so each user's data always lands on the same shard. Sharding solves the problem replication doesn't — when the total dataset is too large for any single machine, no number of full replicas fixes that, since every replica would need to hold everything. The cost: cross-shard queries (joining data that lives on different shards) become much harder.

## CDN caching

A Content Delivery Network caches static assets (images, JS bundles, videos) at edge locations physically close to users, so a user in Mumbai doesn't fetch a static asset from a server in Virginia every time. This reduces latency and offloads traffic from your origin server. CDNs work well for content that's the same for every user and doesn't change often — they're the wrong tool for personalized, frequently-changing data.

## Cache-invalidation strategies

The hard part of any cache (CDN or Redis, see Unit 2.3) is knowing **when** cached data has gone stale. Common strategies: TTL-based expiry (simple, but data can be stale for up to the TTL window), explicit invalidation on write (more accurate, but requires every code path that mutates data to remember to invalidate — easy to miss one), and versioned/cache-busted URLs for static assets (append a content hash to the filename, so a new version is automatically a cache miss).

## Consistent hashing

A hashing technique used for both sharding and load balancing that minimizes redistribution when nodes are added or removed. With naive `hash(key) % number_of_nodes`, adding one node reshuffles almost every key's assignment. Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto a conceptual ring, so adding or removing a node only affects the keys immediately adjacent to it on the ring — a small fraction, not everything. This is why it's the standard technique behind distributed caches and databases that need to scale nodes up and down without a full data reshuffle.

## Practice tip

Practice explaining replication vs. sharding as **two different problems** ("too much traffic" vs. "too much data") — conflating them is one of the most common system design interview mistakes.
lessons.5.4:
# Async & Messaging

Not every operation needs to happen synchronously in the request/response cycle. This unit covers the tools for decoupling "the user needs an immediate response" from "the work actually needs to happen."

## Message queues

A queue sits between a **producer** (something that creates work) and a **consumer** (something that processes it), holding messages until a consumer is ready. This decouples the two: the producer doesn't need the consumer to be available or fast at the moment of sending, it just enqueues and moves on.

```
Producer → [ Queue: order-processing ] → Consumer
```

Example: when a user places an order, the API can immediately respond "order received" while a queued job handles sending the confirmation email, updating inventory, and notifying a warehouse system — none of which the user needs to wait for.

## Why this matters for reliability, not just speed

Queues also add resilience: if a consumer crashes mid-processing, most queue systems (with acknowledgment semantics) redeliver the message instead of losing it. This is a meaningfully different reliability model than a direct synchronous call, which simply fails if the downstream service is down at that exact moment.

## Pub/sub (publish-subscribe)

A related but distinct pattern: a publisher emits an event without knowing (or caring) who's listening, and any number of subscribers can independently receive and react to it.

```
Publisher → topic: "user.signed_up" → Subscriber A (send welcome email)
                                     → Subscriber B (create analytics record)
                                     → Subscriber C (add to CRM)
```

The key difference from a queue: a queue message is typically consumed by **one** worker (work distribution); a pub/sub event can be received by **many** independent subscribers (fan-out/notification). Choose a queue when you want exactly one worker to do a piece of work; choose pub/sub when multiple independent systems all need to react to the same event.

## Event-driven architecture

A broader architectural style where services communicate primarily by emitting and reacting to events, rather than calling each other directly (synchronous request/response). Benefits: services are more decoupled (a new subscriber can be added without touching the publisher), and the system is naturally more resilient to a single service being temporarily down. Costs: harder to trace a request's full path (it's spread across multiple asynchronous event handlers instead of one call stack), and you have to design for eventual consistency — other parts of the system won't reflect an event immediately, only shortly after.

## Recognizing when async/messaging is the right call

Ask: "Does the user need to wait for this specific piece of work to finish before they get a response?" If the answer is no (sending an email, generating a report, updating a search index, notifying a third-party webhook), it's a strong candidate to move off the synchronous request path and into a queue or event. If the user needs the result immediately to proceed (checking whether a payment succeeded), it usually stays synchronous.

## Practice tip

For any "design X" system design question, explicitly separate the request path (what the user waits for) from the background path (what can happen asynchronously afterward) — this separation is often the single most valuable thing you can draw on the whiteboard.
lessons.5.5:
# Classic Design Problems

This unit is where 5.1–5.4's vocabulary gets exercised against specific, commonly-asked problems. The goal isn't to memorize a "correct" design for each — it's to practice the same structured approach on all of them.

## A repeatable approach for any "design X" question

1. **Clarify requirements and scale.** How many users? Reads vs. writes ratio? Is strong consistency required, or is eventual consistency acceptable? Don't skip this — the right answer changes completely depending on scale.
2. **Sketch the high-level components** (client → load balancer → API → database, plus cache/queue where relevant) before diving into any one piece.
3. **Identify the bottleneck** the problem is actually testing, and go deep there.
4. **Name the trade-offs explicitly** as you make choices — this is what separates a strong answer from a list of buzzwords.

## Design a URL shortener

Core challenge: generating short, unique codes for URLs at scale, and looking them up fast on redirect. Approach: a key-value store (code → long URL) is a near-perfect fit — reads (redirects) vastly outnumber writes (new shortened URLs), which argues for a cache in front of the database. Code generation: either a counter converted to base62, or a hash of the URL truncated and checked for collisions. Discuss: custom aliases, expiry, and analytics (click counts) as extensions once the core works.

## Design a rate limiter

Covered in mechanism terms in Unit 5.2 (token bucket, sliding window) — the system design angle adds: where does the rate-limiter state live? A single-instance in-memory counter doesn't work once you have multiple API servers behind a load balancer, because each instance would track its own separate count. The fix is centralizing counters in something shared and fast — Redis is the standard answer, since `INCR` with a TTL gives you an atomic, shared counter across all instances.

## Design a chat app

Core challenge: real-time bidirectional communication. WebSockets (not polling) are the standard answer for low-latency delivery. Discuss: message persistence (a database, separate from the real-time delivery layer), presence/online-status (often a separate lightweight system, since it changes constantly and doesn't need durability), and fan-out for group chats (a message to a group needs to reach every connected member — related to the pub/sub pattern in Unit 5.4).

## Design a news feed

Core challenge: efficiently generating a personalized, ranked feed for millions of users. Two classic strategies: **fan-out on write** (when someone posts, immediately push it into every follower's feed — fast reads, expensive/slow writes for users with huge follower counts) vs. **fan-out on read** (compute the feed at request time by pulling from everyone you follow — cheap writes, more expensive reads). Most real systems use a hybrid: fan-out on write for typical users, fan-out on read for users with huge followings (to avoid a single post fanning out to millions of feeds instantly).

## Design a notification system

Core challenge: reliably delivering notifications across multiple channels (push, email, SMS) without duplicating logic per channel. A queue-based, event-driven design (Unit 5.4) fits naturally: an event ("order shipped") is published once, and separate consumers handle each channel. Discuss: user preferences (which channels they've opted into), deduplication (don't send the same notification twice if an event fires twice), and retry/backoff for failed deliveries.

## Practice tip

Do these out loud, not just in your head — narrate your reasoning as if explaining to an interviewer, and time yourself. The skill being tested is as much "can you communicate a design under time pressure" as "do you know the right components."
